<reason>CON built a tighter, more disciplined case by forcing PRO into a corner: once PRO stipulated that the fragile-site cap does all the conservation work, CON extracted the decisive concession that resident priority produces "no physical effect" on the stone. That single admission gutted PRO's opening framing (correcting a "market failure" that was "consuming the site to exhaustion") and left PRO defending a purely distributive/standing claim. CON then used PRO's own numbers (a 10-20% quota) to show the policy still leaves most residents excluded while cutting peak yield that funds restoration, contrasting it with a levy that reaches all residents and funds the fabric. PRO's closing pivot ("access, not compensation, is what matters") is a reasonable rejoinder but was never fully cashed out against CON's "raffle" framing or the revenue tradeoff, leaving CON's comparative frame ("cap protects, levy funds, quota does neither") as the cleaner, more decisive lens for the judge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 answer to the pressure question (A1/A2 in [B4.1]-[B4.4]), which weaponized PRO's own concession that resident priority has "no physical effect" and PRO's own 10-20% figure to argue the policy helps few residents while shrinking conservation revenue — this exchange most clearly reset the debate in CON's favor.</best_rebuttal>
